toc.title: Path 1: an acute life threat reaction
Path 2: a chronic disruption of connectedness

blocks.p: Trauma is not the event(s) you went through, like surviving a disaster. Nor the events you didn't go through but should have, like developing a healthy attachment with a parent. Trauma is the impact of those things: being stuck in an autonomic nervous system state of defense. Trauma is the inability to access the top of the Polyvagal ladder, [safety](piece:safety-state).

Understanding trauma in this way is significant in light of your new Polyvagal paradigm. This new understanding of trauma can provide an additional layer to that paradigm and new opportunities for building a narrative for one's personal story.

Trauma is the impact of the event or the impact of the lack of events on an individual. There are two general paths to trauma, though they can take many forms. Although the two paths are distinct, overlap may occur.

blocks.h: Path 1: an acute life threat reaction

blocks.p: The "acute life threat reaction" path involves the autonomic nervous system simultaneously entering flight/fight and shutdown activation. However, the individual does not use the sympathetic energy to run or fight due to the perceived or forced immobilization of the circumstance. The immobilization of shutdown locks in or freezes the flight/fight energy. Path 1 is sometimes referred to as "shock trauma" and is associated with "Big T" trauma. Some examples:

Yes, even childhood falls and routine medical procedures. I was dismissive of this when I heard it from Peter Levine. "That's just normal childhood stuff!" But whether it's normal or not is not the point. If the body goes into flight/fight and cannot utilize the energy, this could result in a stuck defensive state. (Though anesthesia and surgeries are hardly "normal childhood stuff" from an evolutionary perspective.)

When sympathetically active, one needs to use the flight/fight activation in one big burst of movement, like lifting or sprinting. However, the immobilization aspect of Path 1 freezes the activation in the system, lingering potentially for years. This individual will have significant difficulty recognizing, feeling, and discharging this lingering activation. They've probably learned how to cope with, reduce, minimize, or numb it. But not how to feel and release it.

The sensations of releasing the stuck flight/fight energy of freeze are intense. When the flight/fight is activated, it often results in not just anxiety but panic, not just anger but rage, not just stress but overwhelm.

This intensity is partially due to the individual's unfamiliarity with feeling and releasing their stuck flight/fight energy. But it's also due to the freezing or locking mechanism of shutdown as part of freeze. Shutdown immobilizes the body, even when it's ready to run or fight. It's like a car's brake: when you hit the brake, the car stops, even if you have your other foot on the gas. The car is ready to mobilize (flight/fight), but the brake keeps it immobile (shutdown). However, the accelerator is still on, and the engine is revving, ready to take off (freeze). To release the stuck flight/fight activation, the immobility of shutdown needs to come off. (The car driver needs to take their foot off the brake.)

Removing the shutdown immobilization is potentially a long process, and it probably won't occur all in one sitting. Instead, the immobilization needs to come off gradually. In other words, the freeze needs to thaw. As the freeze thaws, the frozen flight/fight energy can begin to release a bit at a time.

Think of our driver with their foot on the brake and the accelerator. If they push down hard on both, their engine revs loud and hot, the wheels spin, and the rubber starts to burn on the pavement, leaving a stinky cloud of smoke. If the driver releases their foot from the brake, the car will take off, out of control and likely crash. We don't want that in trauma recovery.

Instead, the driver needs to recognize when there is a very low level of flight/fight activation or freeze. They should recognize the activation before a full-on freeze occurs. Then, they should slowly release their foot from the brake and allow the body to mobilize, using low-level activation. As the brake is slowly released, the car can move forward (mobilize).

If the traumatized individual goes too far, too fast, it may result in a car crash. Retraumatization happens when they attempt to "feel their feelings" or "sit with it" before they are ready. Retraumatization can also occur if a therapist pushes them to share their trauma narrative before they can handle it. Clients who have been through EMDR and TF-CBT often report to me they went into shutdown numbness when they had to share their trauma narratives (even repeatedly).

What does it look like if you trigger a freeze? If more of a frozen fight state exists, the stuck energy could explode when triggered. Exploding frozen fight looks like uncontrollable, blackout anger: rage. This person becomes highly mobilized and aggressive, lashing out at whatever they perceive as a threat. If the frozen energy is more flight-flavored, then it will look like intense, spiraling anxiety: panic. They freeze in place, wide-eyed and stiff-muscled, and feel impending doom.

Thawing is a long process but generally possible. Therapy can be an excellent context for thawing. The therapist should be able to provide safety, both environmentally and interpersonally. Then, they gradually assist the client in strengthening their safety state and eventually climb their Polyvagal ladder out of their stuck defensive state.

Strengthening the safety state is key to trauma recovery. As the safety state strengthens, the shutdown immobilization gradually comes off. Gradually removing shutdown allows the mobilization process while in safety, releasing stuck trauma in Path 1.

blocks.why: Strengthening the safety state is key. This practice is one small piece of that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: Path 1 is probably the underlying cause of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). Just like with PTSD, the individual is stuck in a certain moment or easily triggered into it through aspects reminiscent of the moment. For example, if one survives an assault from a dog pack, their freeze response may be triggered when seeing a dog later in life.

Let's use the car metaphor again: the car is fine until the human triggers it into a freeze when they push the brake and the gas at the same time. Likewise, one may be fine until something in the environment triggers their freeze response connected to the traumatic incident. These environmental triggers may be otherwise benign, having no inherent danger quality to them, like a particular texture or smell.

During these life-threatening freeze events, the body and brain take stock of sensory stimuli. "At the moment a trauma takes place, all of a person's senses automatically focus on the most salient aspect of the threat... [T]hey become... the intrusive image or imprint". The "most salient aspect" of the event is now associated with the traumatic incident. And the next time one is near that stimulus, the same defensive reaction is triggered, even though it's not necessary.

blocks.h: Path 2: a chronic disruption of connectedness

blocks.p: We all have an impulse to connect with other humans. The need for connection never stops, but is even more important in childhood. Children's ventral vagal pathways form and strengthen through connection with safe and reliable caregivers.

A "chronic disruption of connectedness" is when someone's impulse to connect and form a healthy attachment is repeatedly severed or unmet. The individual cannot access and develop their safety pathways because connection is unreliable, unpredictable, or absent. Commonly, someone, like a caregiver or a significant other, abuses or neglects the individual, which cuts off their safety access. This path of trauma can result in chronic stuckness in any of the defensive states.

C-PTSD stands for Complex Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, currently not an officially recognized diagnosis in the 5th edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (the "Bible" for people working in mental health). A core historical element of C-PTSD is repeated, prolonged exposure to traumatic incidents, like in captivity and unable to escape. This can apply to many different scenarios:

All of these involve the victim being under the control of another. They cannot run and cannot fight the captor. The only other option is to shut down. One of these acts is enough to leave someone in a stuck freeze state (Path 1). Repeated acts solidify the freeze state, plus being cut off from safety, along with the total control of the captor (Path 2).

Path 2 is distinct from Path 1. Let's say a young boy survives an attack by a pack of stray dogs. The attack occurs while the kid passes a toy shop on his walk down Main Street. During the attack, his eyes lock onto a painting of a smiling Mario in the toy shop window. He survives the attack, but it leaves him in a stuck freeze state.

If the boy remains stuck in freeze, then dogs, Mario, or even Main Street may continue to trigger his freeze. But he's potentially fine outside any sensory stimuli that connect him to the dog attack. He can live a normal, functioning life, including finding love within himself and for others. What I just described is Path 1.

Now, what about a child who goes through repeated events of abuse, neglect, or ongoing isolation? And what if these are from caregivers who are supposed to provide safety? This is Path 2. This child does not have the chance to develop their safety state. The ventral vagal pathways don't develop the myelination necessary for secure attachment and emotional regulation. This child has little to no capacity to feel safety, trust, or vulnerability. Of course, they are born with the impulse to do so. However, the impulse to connect is repeatedly interrupted through ongoing abuse, neglect, and isolation.

If the impulse to connect is unfulfilled, a defensive state will chronically dominate their existence. This child may live in constant flight, assuming the worst about everyone in life and too anxious to try something new. They may exist in fight and aggressively talk back to their teachers and peers. They may live in shutdown, disconnected from any motivation to succeed academically, instead opting for isolation in their dark room.

Growing up and living a functional life will be much more of a challenge for the person living with Path 2 trauma. They won't identify safety in others. They might identify manipulative individuals as "normal" and gravitate toward those relationships, feeling some level of protection or predictability. They may lack the motivation and discipline to get ahead in life, unable to find purpose or fulfillment from much of anything. Life is potentially very empty and pointless. They may chronically blame others for their life context. (Of course, everyone is unique and will have their own outcomes.)

The above scenarios might seem extreme, but they're not. It's realistic for a child who is not allowed to build their safety state through healthy and predictable connections with safe others. Safety is a complete stranger to their bodies, so much so that they don't recognize it in others or within themselves when it is there. They may be stuck in any defensive state perpetually.

Children have a biological drive to connect to caregivers. If they don't have adults taking care of them, they won't survive. It's just that simple. So they will put up with a lot and still make attempts to connect: or at least hope for a connection. For survival, not because they are actually forgiving or forgetting, but because it's simply a biological imperative to continue to put trust and hope into the people who are their caregivers.

This implicit need and trust in adults is easily misused, abused, and manipulated. Parents and other caregivers must be self-regulated enough to nurture this drive within children. If not, then the child's innate impulse to connect will not develop in the proper direction. They won't develop the myelinated ventral vagal pathways necessary to identify and build healthy relationships in the future. They won't healthily meet expected physical, emotional, cognitive, or interpersonal development milestones.

They will lack the foundation necessary for safety, resulting in a chronic, stuck defensive state. Path 2 trauma individuals may get triggered into severe dysregulation, but they also exist every moment in dysregulation. They constantly struggle to access and maintain their safety state.

blocks.prompt: Can you identify events or contexts in your life that were more likely to result in path 1? How about path 2? (Keep it very light. Yes or no will suffice.)
Is it possible that your stuck state is simply a result of your life's context? And not a reflection of who you are or your worth?
Is more connection and fulfillment possible if you emerge from your stuck defensive state? What might that look like?

blocks.q: "Trauma is the most avoided, ignored, denied, misunderstood, and untreated cause of human suffering." (Levine)
blocks.cite: Levine, P. A. (2005). Healing Trauma: A Pioneering Program for Restoring the Wisdom of Your Body. Sounds True.

blocks.q: "In two sentences: Trauma occurs when we are intensely frightened and are either physically restrained or perceive that we are trapped. We freeze in paralysis and/or collapse in overwhelming helplessness." (Levine)
blocks.cite: Levine, P. A. (2010). In an Unspoken Voice. North Atlantic Books.

blocks.q: "The social engagement system enabled mammals to co-opt some of the features of the vertebrate defense systems to promote social interactions such as play and intimacy. These changes in the autonomic nervous system provided mammals with neural mechanisms to promote the biobehavioral states necessary for caring for offspring, reproducing, and cooperative behavior. In contrast, the adverse behavioral and psychological effects of trauma appear to target a disruption of the social engagement system, its management of defense reactions, and its contribution to co-regulation and cooperative behaviors, including intimacy and play." (Porges)
blocks.cite: Porges, S. W. (2018). Polyvagal theory: A primer. In S. W. Porges & D. Dana (Eds.), Clinical Applications of the Polyvagal Theory: The Emergence of Polyvagal-Informed Therapies (pp. 50–61). W. W. Norton & Company.

blocks.p: My translation: Mammals use their safety state to repurpose defense for prosocial behavior. Trauma messes this up.
